traits: Soft-bodied specks, green, black, or orange, clustered on new growth
Curling, sticky leaves from honeydew feeding
Winged forms have a black head/thorax and pale abdomen
Ladybugs showing up nearby is nature responding to the outbreak

look_alikes.difference: Aphids are soft, pear-shaped, and clustered in the open on new growth; mealybugs are covered in white cottony wax and tucked into stem joints.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the cluster showing whether it has a waxy white coating or is bare-bodied.

copy.what_it_means: Aphids sap plant vigor and leave sticky honeydew that grows black sooty mold. Blast light infestations with water and let ladybugs work; persistent, heavy infestations across many plants are worth treating.
copy.fact: Aphids are born pregnant — generations telescope inside each other, which is how a clean plant is covered by Friday.
copy.blurb: Blast with water, let the ladybugs work; treat only persistent infestations.

tech_notes: ID color morph and host plant. Horticultural oil/insecticidal soap for light cases; systemic for persistent, heavy infestations.

traits: White, cottony wax clusters at stem joints and leaf bases
Sticky honeydew on leaves below the clusters
Ants often run protection patrols nearby, tending the colony
Slow-moving, oval body under the waxy coating, about 3 mm

look_alikes.difference: Mealybugs are stationary, waxy-white, and clustered on the plant; the mealybug destroyer beetle larva looks similar but moves around actively hunting them.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up showing whether the waxy insect is moving and actively hunting versus stationary and feeding.

copy.what_it_means: Ants literally farm mealybugs — guarding the colony and milking the honeydew. Small outbreaks wipe off with soapy water; recurring ones usually ride along with an ant problem worth addressing too.
copy.fact: Ants literally farm them — guarding the herd and milking the honeydew like six-legged dairy farmers.
copy.blurb: Small outbreaks wipe off with soapy water; recurring ones ride on the ant problem.

tech_notes: Check for attending ants; treat ant trail alongside mealybug control. Systemic or horticultural oil per plant/label; wax coating limits contact-spray success.

traits: White waxy spirals laid in concentric circles on palm frond undersides
Sticky honeydew film on cars, pool decks, and furniture below infested trees
Black sooty mold following the sticky film
Adults about 2.5 mm with light brown bands on the wings

look_alikes.difference: Rugose spiraling whitefly lays eggs in a visible spiral, mainly on palms; ficus whitefly doesn't spiral and targets ficus hedges.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaf underside egg pattern, plus which plant it is on.

copy.what_it_means: The spiral pattern is the female's egg-laying signature — like a tiny crop circle under every frond. Trees usually survive, but the sticky fallout zone on patios, pools, and cars makes treatment worthwhile.
copy.fact: The spiral pattern is her egg-laying signature — like a tiny crop circle under every frond.
copy.blurb: Trees usually survive, but the sticky fallout zone makes treatment worth it.

tech_notes: Confirm spiral egg pattern on palm/gumbo limbo/avocado. Systemic soil or trunk treatment outperforms contact sprays; mechanical wash-down helps short-term.

traits: White-to-brown flecking stuck to leaf undersides, mainly camellias and hollies
Yellow blotches (chlorosis) on the corresponding leaf top side
Doesn't wipe off easily — it's cemented in place
Dead scales exude no fluid when pinched, unlike a living insect

look_alikes.difference: Tea scale is flat, brown flecking on leaf undersides of camellias and hollies; Florida wax scale is a raised, pinkish-white waxy bump on stems.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the scale shape (flat vs. raised) and which plant part it is on.

copy.what_it_means: Adult scales cement themselves in place and live under a waxy shell for life, which is why a quick spray often doesn't reach them. A technician picks the approach — product choice, coverage on leaf undersides, timing and follow-up — based on how established the infestation is and the plant's condition.
copy.fact: Adult scales never move again once they settle — they cement themselves down and live under that shell for the rest of their life.
copy.blurb: The waxy shell is why timing and coverage on leaf undersides matter as much as which product is used.

tech_notes: Confirm flat brown armor on leaf underside plus matching top-side chlorosis. Evaluate product choice (horticultural oil applied to leaf undersides is a recognized option), timing, plant condition and follow-up rather than one fixed treatment.

traits: Tiny (about 1/16 inch), moth-like white insect that flies up in a cloud when a ficus hedge is disturbed
Undersides of ficus leaves dotted with small, flat, pale oval nymphs and pupae
Heavy yellowing and leaf drop on ficus hedges, sometimes leaving branches bare within weeks
Sticky honeydew and black sooty mold build up on leaves and anything below the hedge

look_alikes.difference: Ficus whitefly sticks to ficus and leaves no pattern in its wax; rugose spiraling whitefly leaves spiral-shaped rings of white wax and also attacks palms
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaf underside checking for spiral rings of wax versus a random scatter

copy.what_it_means: A fast-spreading pest of ficus hedges that can strip a hedge of leaves within weeks once it takes hold. A ficus hedge that's suddenly yellowing and dropping leaves is worth a tree & shrub look before it goes bare.
copy.fact: It was first found in Florida in 2007 and spread across the state within a couple of years, mainly by attacking the ubiquitous ficus hedge.

tech_notes: Confirm host is Ficus (especially F. benjamina) and check leaf undersides for nymphs/pupae; systemic treatment timing matters since defoliation can be rapid once established.

traits: Tiny, white, pear-shaped scales that build up into a thick white crust on fronds and stems
Orange insect body and eggs visible if the white waxy covering is scraped away
Fronds show yellow or bleached spots first, then turn brown and dry-looking
Found mainly on king sago and other cycads (not true palms), often on the underside of leaflets first

look_alikes.difference: Cycad scale forms a flat white crust only on cycads; Florida wax scale is a raised pinkish-white dome found on citrus, holly and many other shrubs, not cycads
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the scale and a wider shot of the whole plant to confirm it's a cycad

copy.what_it_means: This scale can kill a king sago that goes untreated, since it also colonizes roots underground and keeps rebuilding its white crust after dead scales are cleaned off. A cycad turning bleached or brown and crusty is worth a prompt look.
copy.fact: This scale first appeared on cycads in a Miami nursery in 1996 and spread statewide within a few years.

tech_notes: Confirm host is a cycad (not a palm) and check for root-zone colonization in heavy infestations; horticultural oil coverage and repeat treatments are typically needed since dead scales persist visually.

traits: Small (1/8 to 1/6 inch), dome-shaped bump coated in thick pinkish-white to gray wax
Young scales look star-shaped from ridges in the wax before rounding out
Found fixed in clusters on twigs and leaf undersides of citrus, holly and other shrubs
Sticky honeydew and black sooty mold often build up on leaves below an infestation

look_alikes.difference: Florida wax scale is a rounded pinkish-white waxy dome on leaves/twigs; lobate lac scale is flatter, reddish-brown, X-shaped, blending into bark
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of one scale's shape and color against the twig or leaf it's on

copy.what_it_means: A common, slow-moving scale that mostly causes cosmetic honeydew and sooty mold rather than serious plant decline. Light numbers are worth watching; heavier clusters on citrus or holly are worth a tree & shrub look.
copy.fact: Once a young crawler settles and starts building its waxy dome, it never moves again for the rest of its life.

tech_notes: Confirm crawler stage timing for oil/soap treatment windows; check for ant activity tending honeydew, which can mean populations are being protected from natural predators.

traits: Tiny (about 1/16 inch), reddish-brown scale shaped like an X or bow tie, blending in with bark
Packed in dense rows and clusters along twigs and small branches
Found on a very wide range of woody shrubs and trees, not just one plant type
Heavy infestations bring branch dieback along with thick black sooty mold underneath

look_alikes.difference: Lobate lac scale is flatter, reddish-brown and X-shaped, blending into bark; Florida wax scale is a rounded pinkish-white waxy dome on leaves and twigs
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of one scale's shape and color against the twig or leaf it's on

copy.what_it_means: This scale spreads to an unusually wide range of shrubs and trees and can build up so densely on branches that it kills them outright. Dense reddish-brown clusters on twigs, especially with dieback starting, are worth a prompt tree & shrub look.
copy.fact: It has been documented feeding on several hundred different plant species since showing up in Broward County in 1999, an unusually broad host range for a scale insect.

tech_notes: Confirm the X/bow-tie shape and dense packing along twigs; document extent of branch dieback and host range affected, since this species can move to nearby unrelated plants.

review.notes: Source corrected to IN471 (the actual Lobate Lac Scale Featured Creature). IN471 documents spread from Broward County (1999) through Miami-Dade and Palm Beach; UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions broadens this to 'a potentially damaging landscape pest in southern Florida.' Neither source names a Southwest Florida county, so SWFL-specific density stays unconfirmed; range is kept at 'occasional' as the cautious, source-consistent regional default (southern Florida generally), not a specific SWFL claim. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Black, powdery or crusty coating over the tops and undersides of leaves, twigs, and surfaces underneath the plant
Wipes or flakes off in dry, sooty smudges rather than staining like ground-in dirt
Sticky, clear honeydew or its residue may be visible nearby, even when the sap-feeding insects are no longer present
Leaves underneath look shaded and grow more slowly, but the mold itself isn't infecting the plant

look_alikes.difference: Sooty mold is a black coating that wipes or flakes off the leaf surface; lobate lac scale is fixed reddish-brown bumps you'd have to scrape off
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up trying to wipe the black material with a finger or cloth to see if it comes off as soot or stays fixed as a bump

copy.what_it_means: Sooty mold itself doesn't harm the plant directly; it's just growing on sugary honeydew left behind by a sap-feeding insect. The real fix is finding and treating whichever aphid, mealybug, scale or whitefly is feeding above it.
copy.fact: The fungi that cause sooty mold grow only on the surface and never actually infect the leaf underneath.

tech_notes: Identify the causal sap-feeder (check for aphids, mealybugs, scale, or whitefly on the plant or overhanging tree) before treating; mold typically clears once the insect source is controlled and washed off.

review.notes: sign_of list is illustrative of common causes, not exhaustive; any sap-feeding, honeydew-producing insect on the plant or an overhanging tree can be the true source. Returned to draft after correcting the visible trait so an old honeydew deposit does not require live feeders to remain visible; owner re-approval is required. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Extremely tiny (under 1/50 inch), pale yellow, slender insect, hard to see without a hand lens
New leaves, buds and flowers look scorched, bronzed, curled or twisted, worst at the growing tips
Damage shows up on the newest growth first, unlike spider mite damage on older leaves
Found tucked inside furled new leaves and flower buds rather than out in the open

look_alikes.difference: Chilli thrips damage concentrates on curled new growth and buds; spider mite damage is fine stippling with webbing on older leaves
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the newest leaf tips versus the underside of an older leaf, checking for webbing or tiny moving specks

copy.what_it_means: A pest so small it's usually diagnosed by its damage rather than the insect itself: scorched, curled new growth on roses, viburnum and many other ornamentals. Repeated dieback on new flush across a plant is worth a tree & shrub look.
copy.fact: Despite its name, it attacks far more than chilli peppers; roses and viburnum hedges are common targets in home landscapes.

tech_notes: Confirm damage pattern on newest growth and inspect furled leaves/buds with a hand lens for tiny yellow larvae; distinguish from spider mite and herbicide-drift symptoms.

traits: Extremely tiny (pinhead-sized or smaller) reddish, greenish or yellowish specks, easiest to see in groups
Fine silk webbing on the underside of leaves and between stems in heavier infestations
Leaves show a fine, light stippling or a bronzed, bleached look rather than solid brown patches
Tapping a leaf over white paper knocks loose tiny specks that crawl, confirming mites rather than dust

look_alikes.difference: Spider mite damage is fine stippling with webbing on older leaves; chilli thrips damage concentrates on curled, scorched new growth and buds
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the underside of an older leaf checking for webbing or tiny moving specks, versus the newest leaf tips

copy.what_it_means: A hot, dry-weather pest that thrives on stressed plants and can be knocked back with a strong hose spray at low numbers. Light stippling is worth watching; heavy webbing or bronzed leaves on a shrub or tree is worth a closer look.
copy.fact: A single female can start an infestation of hundreds within a couple of weeks in warm weather, since spider mites develop so quickly.

tech_notes: Confirm with a hand lens or paper-tap test; heat and drought stress worsen outbreaks, so irrigation/plant health is part of the fix alongside any miticide.

review.notes: Peak months follow the cited 'hot, dry summer and fall' pattern for twospotted spider mite; Florida's summer is also rainy season, which can knock populations down, so actual SWFL peak timing may vary by year.

traits: Small (about 1/8 inch), mottled tan-brown, wedge-shaped insect that feeds with its rear end raised at roughly a 30 to 45 degree angle
A living adult looks dusty from a whitish, waxy coating over its body
Nymphs are yellow-orange with red eyes and trail curly, white waxy tubules
Found clustered on new citrus flush (young leaf growth), not on older hardened leaves

look_alikes.difference: Psyllid feeds tilted up at a steep angle and nymphs trail curly waxy tubules; aphids sit flatter on the leaf and lack those curly tubules
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up from the side of the insect on the stem to check its feeding angle, plus a look at any nymphs for curly threads

copy.what_it_means: This insect itself does only minor feeding damage, but it spreads citrus greening disease, which has devastated citrus trees across Florida. Finding it on a backyard citrus tree's new growth is worth a look, especially if the tree also shows blotchy, yellow leaves.
copy.fact: The bacteria it spreads move so slowly inside a tree that trees can look healthy for a year or more before greening symptoms show up.

tech_notes: Confirm feeding angle and waxy nymph tubules on new flush; note any blotchy mottled leaf yellowing (possible HLB/citrus greening) for follow-up, since this psyllid is the primary HLB vector in Florida.

review.notes: disease_vector safety flag set to false since it vectors a plant disease (citrus greening/HLB), not a human or pet disease; flagged here so the owner can confirm that's the intended use of that field.

traits: Small (about 1/8 inch), pink body showing through a thin, patchy white waxy coating
Males are smaller, winged, and trail two long white waxy tail filaments
Found in dense clusters on new growth, leaf undersides and flower buds, especially on hibiscus
Feeding twists and stunts new growth into a bushy, deformed 'witch's broom' look at branch tips

look_alikes.difference: Pink mealybug fluid is pink when crushed and causes twisted 'witch's broom' growth; common mealybugs are colorless and don't cause that twisting
look_alikes.next_photo: Gently press one on a white paper towel to check fluid color, plus a photo of the twisted new-growth tip

safety_line: A regulated invasive pest with an unusually wide host range; note where you saw it so the sighting can be reported and tracked.

copy.what_it_means: This mealybug attacks an unusually wide range of ornamentals and fruit trees and can quickly deform new growth into a tangled 'witch's broom.' Twisted new growth with pink-tinged clusters underneath is worth a report and a tree & shrub look.
copy.fact: It was first found in Florida in Broward County in 2002 and is now managed mainly with the help of a tiny introduced parasitic wasp.

tech_notes: Confirm pink body fluid and witch's-broom deformity on new growth; this is a regulated pest of concern, so document and follow current agency reporting guidance for suspected finds outside its known range.

review.notes: SWFL presence confirmed this session: UF/IFAS EDIS IN156 documents first Florida detection in Broward County (2002), then Miami-Dade, with expectation of statewide spread; separately, a UF/IFAS Collier County Extension "Pest Alert!" (Doug Caldwell, Commercial Landscape Horticulture Extension, Collier County) exists specifically warning Collier County residents about PHM, with a local Extension helpline and Plant Clinic contact for suspected finds -- this is direct evidence the local Collier County (SWFL) Extension office treats it as a real, present concern in this catalog's own service area, not just a southeast-Florida phenomenon. Range 'occasional' is consistent with a recognized-but-not-yet-dominant SWFL presence.

traits: New ficus leaves roll or fold tightly along the midrib into a curled gall
Sunken purplish-red spots on the tender new leaves
Curled leaves turn tough and yellow as they age
Small black thrips and pale larvae live inside the rolled leaf

look_alikes.difference: Ficus whitefly causes yellowing and leaf drop with pale nymphs on flat leaf undersides; Cuban laurel thrips cause tightly curled, purple-spotted new leaves.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a curled leaf and a flat leaf underside on the same hedge.

look_alikes.difference: Chilli thrips scorch and bronze new growth without rolling it into tight galls; Cuban laurel thrips roll leaves into a tube with dark thrips inside.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a curled new leaf, then a photo of the leaf gently unrolled.

copy.what_it_means: Tightly curled new leaves with purple spots on a Ficus microcarpa hedge or tree can suggest Cuban laurel thrips, mostly a cosmetic problem. A photo cannot confirm it; a technician unrolls a curled leaf to look for the thrips inside.
copy.fact: Cuban laurel thrips live and breed inside the rolled leaf, so a full generation can develop within a single curled gall.

tech_notes: Unroll a curled leaf and look for black adult thrips and pale larvae inside; the damage is mainly cosmetic. Check that the plant is Ficus microcarpa (Cuban laurel), the main host.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). IN599 says breeding is continuous through the year with no monthly calendar, so peak_months [3, 4, 5, 9, 10] come from the owner brief.

verification.note: From the owner brief; IN599 documents year-round breeding (about 30 days per generation) but no monthly peak.

traits: Flat, white to grayish crusts stuck to leaves and stems
Yellow spots on the upper leaf surface, larger than the scales beneath
Heavy infestations can cause yellowing and leaf drop, especially on croton
Found on many hosts, including croton, gardenia and magnolia

look_alikes.difference: Cycad aulacaspis scale coats the fronds of king sago and other cycads; magnolia white scale is found on broadleaf shrubs such as croton and gardenia.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the whole plant, then a close-up of the crusts on one leaf.

look_alikes.difference: Tea scale is brown flecking on leaf undersides, mostly camellia and holly; magnolia white scale forms white crusts on leaves and stems of many hosts.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the crust color and whether it is on the leaf top, underside or stem.

copy.what_it_means: White crusts on the leaves and stems of croton, gardenia or magnolia can suggest magnolia white scale, and heavy infestations can cause leaf drop. A technician checks whether the scales are alive and whether live crawlers are present before choosing a next step.
copy.fact: False oleander scale is a poor name for it; UF/IFAS records more than 100 host plants in Florida, including croton, gardenia and magnolia.

tech_notes: Crush a crust to see whether the scale underneath is alive (dead scales stay on the plant); check for live crawlers, since they are the vulnerable stage. Note the host and any leaf drop.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). peak_months left empty: no Florida monthly peak is documented in IN306.

traits: Sticky, shiny honeydew coating leaves and stems, and anything under the tree
Black sooty mold growing on the honeydew
Pale to bright yellow aphids with black markings, feeding on the leaf surface
Found on crape myrtle, often building up as the season warms

look_alikes.difference: Other aphids are green, black or orange and cluster on many plants; crapemyrtle aphids are pale yellow with black spots and stay on crape myrtle.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the insects on a leaf, and a wide shot showing the plant is crape myrtle.

look_alikes.difference: Sooty mold is only the black coating; the crapemyrtle aphid is the sap-feeding insect whose honeydew feeds it.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaf surface checking for small yellow insects among the black coating.

copy.what_it_means: Sticky leaves with a black sooty coating on a crape myrtle can suggest crapemyrtle aphid, which is mostly a cosmetic problem. A technician checks the leaves for the small yellow aphids that leave the honeydew behind.
copy.fact: The black coating on crape myrtle is a mold growing on aphid honeydew, so it often shows up before anyone spots the small yellow insects.

tech_notes: Look for pale yellow aphids with black markings on the leaf surface; the honeydew and sooty mold usually show first. UF/IFAS notes populations typically escape natural enemies in late July and August, so peak_months may run later than listed.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). Owner brief placed the aphids on leaf undersides; IN663 describes them feeding on the upper leaf surface, so the entry follows the source.

verification.note: From the owner brief. IN663 says populations escape natural enemies near the end of July and early August in Florida, so the peak may include August.

traits: Bronzed or russeted, rough-looking rind on citrus fruit
Damage on young fruit can look like rough, sharkskin-like russeting
Damage is mostly to the surface of the rind; the fruit inside is usually fine
Mites are far too small to see without a hand lens

look_alikes.difference: Spider mites stipple and web leaves; citrus rust mites mark the fruit rind (and sometimes leaves) with bronzing or russeting and no webbing.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the fruit rind and of a nearby leaf underside, checking for webbing.

look_alikes.difference: Wax scale forms raised, waxy pinkish bumps on twigs and leaves; rust mite damage is a flat bronzed or rough discoloration of the rind.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the rind and a nearby twig, checking for raised waxy bumps.

copy.what_it_means: A bronzed or rough, russeted rind on citrus fruit can suggest citrus rust mite, which usually affects how the fruit looks rather than what is inside. A photo cannot confirm it; a technician checks the fruit surface with a hand lens.
copy.fact: Citrus rust mites are far too small to see unaided, so the bronzed or russeted rind is usually the first sign anyone notices.

tech_notes: Check the fruit surface with a 10x hand lens; damage is mainly cosmetic on fruit for home use. UF/IFAS reports populations rising in May to July.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). Source is the commercial citrus production guide; months match its May-July rise and possible late-October increase.
